summary.title: Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning tunneling microscopy
summary.authors: P. Nemes – Incze, Z. Kónya, I. Kiricsi, Á. Pekker, Z.E. Horváth, K. Kamarás, L.P. Biró
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the critical challenge of sample instability in scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) measurements of functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Functional groups on CNT surfaces reduce contact area with substrates, allowing the STM tip to displace or 'clean out' the nanotubes during scanning, which inhibits reliable atomic-resolution imaging and spectroscopy. The authors propose a simple immobilization technique: incorporating functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) into a few-layer graphene (FLG) composite, effectively creating a buckypaper. This clamping mechanism restricts tube movement, enabling reproducible Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS) measurements. The MWCNTs were functionalized via a three-step chemical process involving acid oxidation, conversion to acid chlorides, and reaction with diaminopropane to create covalent cross-links. Using this stable composite, the researchers acquired energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps (dI/dV) at various bias voltages. The results reveal distinct electronic regions on the nanotubes: graphitic regions with symmetric dI/dV curves indicating p-doping (Fermi level shift ~0.25 eV) due to acid adsorption; low-conductance regions corresponding to heavily functionalized or defective sites where the sp2 lattice is destroyed; and asymmetric dI/dV regions suggesting local charge transfer or impurity states. Crucially, atomic-resolution STM images show that functionalization and defect creation preferentially follow the zigzag crystallographic direction of the nanotube circumference. This work demonstrates that CITS on immobilized CNTs provides superior insight into local doping, charge transfer, and crystallographic dependence of functionalization compared to topography alone, opening avenues for in situ studies of gas sensing mechanisms.

claims.description: Immobilizing functionalized CNTs in a few-layer graphene composite enables stable, atomic-resolution STM and CITS measurements.
Functionalization and defect creation on large-diameter MWCNTs preferentially follow the zigzag crystallographic direction.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the critical challenge of sample instability in scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) measurements of functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNTs). Functional groups on CNT surfaces reduce contact area with substrates, allowing the STM tip to displace or 'clean out' the nanotubes during scanning, which inhibits reliable atomic-resolution imaging and spectroscopy. The authors propose a simple immobilization technique: incorporating functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) into a few-layer graphene (FLG) composite, effectively creating a buckypaper. This clamping mechanism restricts tube movement, enabling reproducible Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS) measurements. The MWCNTs were functionalized via a three-step chemical process involving acid oxidation, conversion to acid chlorides, and reaction with diaminopropane to create covalent cross-links. Using this stable composite, the researchers acquired energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps (dI/dV) at various bias voltages. The results reveal distinct electronic regions on the nanotubes: graphitic regions with symmetric dI/dV curves indicating p-doping (Fermi level shift ~0.25 eV) due to acid adsorption; low-conductance regions corresponding to heavily functionalized or defective sites where the sp2 lattice is destroyed; and asymmetric dI/dV regions suggesting local charge transfer or impurity states. Crucially, atomic-resolution STM images show that functionalization and defect creation preferentially follow the zigzag crystallographic direction of the nanotube circumference. This work demonstrates that CITS on immobilized CNTs provides superior insight into local doping, charge transfer, and crystallographic dependence of functionalization compared to topography alone, opening avenues for in situ studies of gas sensing mechanisms.

Research Context
Sidewall functionalization of CNTs is a versatile tool to change electronic properties. Spectroscopic methods are global probes, lacking spatial resolution. STM provides spatially resolved information down to the atomic scale. A key bottleneck in STM mapping of functionalized CNTs is sample stability. Functional groups decrease contact area, weakening anchoring forces to the substrate. The STM tip can exert forces that move CNTs in the fast scan direction. Previous methods like chemical bonding to substrates may perturb electronic structure.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to map functionalized regions on CNTs with atomic precision. The hypothesis is that immobilizing CNTs in a graphene composite enables stable CITS. The method should allow measurement of energy resolved tunneling conductance maps. The goal is to shed light on doping and charge transfer. The study investigates the dependence of defect creation on crystallographic orientation. It is hypothesized that functionalization may prefer specific crystallographic directions.

Methodological Details
Multiwalled CNTs were prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene. The catalyst used was alumina supported Co/Fe. Functionalization involved a three-step process starting with H2SO4/HNO3 treatment. The first step attached –OH and –COOH groups to the outer wall. The second step involved stirring in SOCl2 to form –COCl groups. The final step used diaminopropane to connect functional groups. This resulted in covalently interconnected MWCNTs. The immobilization was achieved by sandwiching CNTs between few layer graphite flakes. The composite was created by mixing CNTs with exfoliated graphite in isopropyl alcohol. The suspension was filtered through a 200 nm polycarbonate membrane. STM measurements were performed using a Multimode III SPM (Veeco). A Pt/Ir (80:20) wire was used for the STM probe. TEM measurements were done using a Philips CM20 microscope at 200 keV.

Procedures And Architectures
The CITS mode was used to acquire STM images and STS curves. STS data was processed using Scilab for extraction of individual curves. Atomic resolution images were acquired using 500 pA tunneling current. The bias voltage for atomic resolution was 100 mV. STM topography and CITS images used 300 pA tunneling current. The bias voltage for topography and CITS was 300 mV. Tunneling conductance maps were obtained by taking the first derivative of STS curves. Conductance values were displayed at specific bias voltages like -160 mV. The composite was placed on the STM sample holder with carbon colloid paste.

Key Results
The dI/dV maps show regions of high and low conductance on the nanotubes. High conductance regions exhibit graphitic dI/dV curves with symmetric minima. The LDOS minimum is shifted to positive bias, indicating p-doping. The global p-doping level corresponds to a Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV. Low conductance regions have highly asymmetrical dI/dV curves. Low conductance is attributed to destruction of the sp2 π electron lattice. Atomic resolution was not possible in low conductance regions. Functionalized regions appear as protrusions on the nanotube surface. Functionalized regions follow the zigzag direction along the nanotube circumference. Superstructure patterns indicate electron scattering between non-equivalent K points. Asymmetric dI/dV curves in some regions suggest impurity states or charge transfer.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The p-doping is attributed to acid molecule adsorption and oxygen-containing adsorbents. Low conductance regions indicate complete alteration of the graphite lattice. The preference for the zigzag direction supports theories of directional oxidation. Charge transfer between the nanotube and functional groups causes local Coulomb potentials. CITS provides local information that topography alone cannot reveal. This technique allows for in situ studies of gas sensing mechanisms.

Contradictions And Limitations
The interpretation of low conductance regions is not straightforward. The electronic structure of heavily damaged sp2 lattices is unknown. The origin of asymmetry in some dI/dV curves is not clear. The method requires specific chemical compatibility for immobilization. Chemical bonds in other immobilization methods may perturb electronic structure.

Claims
Immobilizing functionalized CNTs in a few-layer graphene composite enables stable, atomic-resolution STM and CITS measurements. The composite restricts nanotube movement during scanning. Reproducible CITS measurements were achieved on the composite. The method is not applicable if chemical binding is required. This technique is widely applicable to various functionalized nanotubes.
Functionalization and defect creation on large-diameter MWCNTs preferentially follow the zigzag crystallographic direction. Atomic resolution images show functionalized bands along the zigzag direction. This provides experimental evidence for directional oxidation reactions. Only a few previous STM studies showed such correlation. This supports models of CNT unzipping to graphene nanoribbons.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compares pristine and functionalized samples via Raman and ATR-IR. The D peak intensity increased relative to the G peak after functionalization. ATR-IR spectra show peaks for –OH, –COOH, and –NH groups.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates CNT movement and cleaning by the STM tip. Figure 2 shows the functionalization scheme and spectroscopic characterization. Figure 3 displays the CNT-FLG composite and TEM images. Figure 4 presents STM images and tunneling conductance maps. Figure 5 shows atomic resolution STM and conductance maps at -225 mV. Figure 6 details dI/dV maps at various bias voltages and LDOS minimum map.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a stable immobilization method for STM/CITS of functionalized CNTs. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of zigzag-directional functionalization and local doping maps. 3. The future path involves in situ studies of gas sensing and adsorption processes.
